title: LLM-assisted writing in biomedical papers
dek: A corpus-level estimate says language-model assistance is already widespread in biomedical publishing; revision and replication will show how much confidence that number deserves.

canonicalSubject.name: LLM-assisted writing in PubMed Central papers

trackingTerms: Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing
whyTracked: The estimate is consequential, method-dependent, and unusually easy to revisit through preprint revisions, peer review, independent replication, and policy responses.

current.assessment: The public evidence remains a single preprint and reporting derived from it. The 89 percent figure is a corpus-level estimate of LLM-associated vocabulary, not a detector for individual papers, and no independent replication was found during admission review.
current.nextReviewTrigger: Review immediately for a revised preprint, peer-reviewed publication, independent replication, methodological critique, or a major publishing-policy change explicitly tied to prevalence evidence.

openQuestions: Will peer review or independent replication materially revise the estimated prevalence?
How much of the detected assistance is translation or editing rather than generation of scientific claims?
Can future estimators separate direct model use from human adoption or avoidance of model-associated vocabulary?

watchFor.trigger: The authors release a revised version, journal article, correction, or methodological response.
An independent group tests the estimator on PubMed Central or another large scholarly corpus.

watchFor.description: Policy response tied to population-level evidence
watchFor.trigger: A major publisher or research body cites prevalence evidence when changing LLM-use disclosure or authorship policy.

observations.headline: Point-zero observation
observations.summary: A preprint estimated that 89 percent of sampled PubMed Central papers published in December 2025 contained signs of LLM-assisted writing or editing somewhere in their full text, while emphasizing that the method cannot classify an individual paper.

sources.title: Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing
Staggering 90% of biomedical papers now show signs of AI help

observations.headline: Admitted to The Wake
observations.summary: Admitted because a prominent quantitative estimate is still provisional and has clear paths to revision, replication, and policy consequence; the admission review found the arXiv record still at its initial public version.
